title: The Transformer Architecture
summary: The transformer combines self-attention, positional encodings, and feedforward layers into a highly parallelizable architecture. Because it processes all tokens at once and scales well with data and compute, it became the backbone of GPT, BERT, and e
content:
# The Transformer Architecture ##### The paper that fit on eight pages In June 2017, eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research published a paper with a title that reads like a provocation: *Attention Is All You Need*. The claim was that you could delete recurrence entirely. No LSTM, no GRU, no sequential hidden state. Just attention, some feedforward layers, and a trick for encoding position. The results were good but not overwhelming — a couple of BLEU points on English-German translation. What was overwhelming was the *training time*. The previous state of the art took weeks on multiple GPUs. The transformer base model trained in twelve hours on eight GPUs. That was the actual breakthrough, and it took a while for people to see it. **Because attention processes all positions simultaneously, transformers parallelise across the sequence dimension.** An RNN with 1,000 tokens needs 1,000 sequential steps that no amount of hardware can compress. A transformer does them all at once. Parallelism made scale affordable. Scale made GPT-3 possible. Everything since — ChatGPT, Claude, Llama, Gemini — is this architecture, made larger. Today you learn every component and why it is there. ##### The full picture ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Input tokens"] --> B["Token embedding"] B --> C["+ Positional encoding"] C --> D["Encoder block × N"] D --> D1["Multi-head self-attention"] D1 --> D2["Add & LayerNorm"] D2 --> D3["Feedforward network"] D3 --> D4["Add & LayerNorm"] D4 --> E["Encoder output"] F["Output tokens
(shifted right)"] --> G["Token embedding
+ positional"] G --> H["Decoder block × N"] H --> H1["Masked self-attention"] H1 --> H2["Add & LayerNorm"] H2 --> H3["Cross-attention
to encoder output"] E --> H3 H3 --> H4["Add & LayerNorm"] H4 --> H5["Feedforward network"] H5 --> H6["Add & LayerNorm"] H6 --> I["Linear → Softmax"] I --> J["Next-token probabilities"] ``` The original paper used both halves. Modern practice has mostly split them: | Type | Uses | Examples | Good at | |---|---|---|---| | **Encoder-only** | Bidirectional attention | BERT, RoBERTa | Understanding: classification, NER, embeddings | | **Decoder-only** | Causal masked attention | GPT, Llama, Claude | Generation | | **Encoder-decoder** | Both, with cross-attention | T5, BART, Whisper | Transformation: translation, summarisation | **Decoder-only dominates today.** It turns out that if you make next-token prediction good enough, it subsumes almost every other task. ##### Positional encoding Here is the problem attention creates. Self-attention is **permutation-invariant**: shuffle the input tokens and the outputs shuffle correspondingly, but each token's representation is unchanged. Attention sees a *set*, not a sequence. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would be identical. Unacceptable. The fix is to add position information to the embeddings before the first layer. The original paper used fixed sinusoids: $$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$ ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt def sinusoidal_encoding(max_len, d_model): pos = np.arange(max_len)[:, None] i = np.arange(d_model)[None, :] angle = pos / np.power(10_000, (2 * (i // 2)) / d_model) pe = np.zeros((max_len, d_model)) pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angle[:, 0::2]) pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angle[:, 1::2]) return pe pe = sinusoidal_encoding(100, 128) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4)) im = ax.imshow(pe.T, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu") ax.set_xlabel("Position in sequence"); ax.set_ylabel("Embedding dimension") ax.set_title("Each position gets a unique sinusoidal fingerprint", loc="left") fig.colorbar(im) ``` Why sinusoids rather than just the integer position? Three reasons. The values stay bounded in [−1, 1], so they do not swamp the token embeddings. Each position gets a unique pattern across dimensions — low dimensions oscillate fast, high dimensions slowly, like the digits of a binary counter. And crucially, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a **linear function** of $PE_{pos}$, so the model can learn relative offsets, and it extrapolates somewhat to sequence lengths never seen in training. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model, max_len=5000, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model) pos = torch.arange(max_len).unsqueeze(1).float() div = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * (-np.log(10_000.0) / d_model)) pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos * div) pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos * div) self.register_buffer("pe", pe.unsqueeze(0)) # not a parameter def forward(self, x): return self.dropout(x + self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]) ``` Modern models mostly use alternatives. **Learned** positional embeddings (BERT, GPT-2) are simply a trainable table. **RoPE** (rotary position embedding), used in Llama, Mistral, and most recent models, rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position — encoding relative position directly inside the attention computation, and extrapolating far better to long contexts. **ALiBi** adds a distance-based penalty to attention scores. The principle is unchanged: attention needs position injected from outside. ##### Feedforward layers After attention, each position passes through a small MLP — applied independently and identically to every position: $$\text{FFN}(x) = W_2 \cdot \text{activation}(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2$$ ```python class FeedForward(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model=512, d_ff=2048, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), # expand 4× nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model), # project back nn.Dropout(dropout), ) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) ``` The expansion ratio is conventionally 4× — 512 → 2048 → 512. **Why is this here?** Attention is fundamentally a weighted average: it *mixes* information across positions but applies no per-position non-linear transformation. The FFN provides that. The clean division of labour: **attention moves information between positions; the FFN processes it within a position.** A surprising fact worth knowing: the FFN holds roughly **two-thirds of a transformer's parameters**. In GPT-3, attention is the famous part but the feedforward layers are where most of the weights live. Recent interpretability work suggests they function something like a key-value memory storing factual associations. ##### Residual connections and layer normalisation Every sublayer is wrapped: $$\text{output} = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))$$ **Residual connections** — the `+ x` — give gradients a direct path backwards, exactly as in ResNet from Day 17. Without them, a 12-layer transformer would suffer the Day 14 vanishing gradient problem. With them, GPT-3's 96 layers train fine. This is arguably as important as attention itself. **LayerNorm** normalises across the feature dimension *within each token*, unlike BatchNorm which normalises across the batch: ```python x = torch.randn(2, 10, 512) # (batch, tokens, features) ln = nn.LayerNorm(512) # normalises over the 512 features, per token out = ln(x) print(out.mean(dim=-1).abs().max().item()) # ~0 print(out.std(dim=-1).mean().item()) # ~1 ``` LayerNorm is used because it is independent of batch size and handles variable-length sequences — both essential for text. **Pre-norm versus post-norm** is a detail with real consequences: ```python # Post-norm (original 2017 paper) x = self.norm1(x + self.attn(x)) x = self.norm2(x + self.ffn(x)) # Pre-norm (every modern model) x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)) ``` Pre-norm keeps a clean, un-normalised residual path from input to output, which makes deep stacks far more stable. Post-norm models need careful learning-rate warm-up or they diverge. **Every large model since roughly GPT-2 uses pre-norm.** ##### Assembling a block ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class TransformerBlock(nn.Module): """Pre-norm decoder block, nanoGPT style.""" def __init__(self, d_model=384, n_heads=6, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model) self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d_model, n_heads, dropout=dropout, batch_first=True) self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model) self.ffn = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d_model, 4 * d_model), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d_model, d_model), nn.Dropout(dropout), ) def forward(self, x, attn_mask=None): h = self.norm1(x) a, _ = self.attn(h, h, h, attn_mask=attn_mask, need_weights=False) x = x + a # residual 1 x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)) # residual 2 return x class TinyGPT(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model=384, n_heads=6, n_layers=6, block_size=256, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.block_size = block_size self.tok_emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model) self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(block_size, d_model) self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout) self.blocks = nn.ModuleList( [TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, dropout) for _ in range(n_layers)] ) self.norm_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model) self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False) self.head.weight = self.tok_emb.weight # weight tying def forward(self, idx): B, T = idx.shape pos = torch.arange(T, device=idx.device) x = self.drop(self.tok_emb(idx) + self.pos_emb(pos)) causal = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=idx.device), diagonal=1).bool() for block in self.blocks: x = block(x, attn_mask=causal) return self.head(self.norm_f(x)) # (B, T, vocab_size) model = TinyGPT(vocab_size=65) print(f"{sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,} parameters") out = model(torch.randint(0, 65, (2, 32))) print(out.shape) # torch.Size([2, 32, 65]) ``` **Weight tying** — sharing the embedding matrix with the output projection — saves a large number of parameters and usually improves quality, since both matrices are mapping between token space and embedding space. ##### Why transformers scale Four properties, and together they explain the last eight years. **1. Parallelism during training.** All positions computed simultaneously. This is the one that matters most — it converts a sequential problem into a matrix multiplication, and GPUs are matrix multiplication machines. **2. Constant path length.** Any two positions communicate in one attention hop, O(1), versus O(n) for an RNN. Long-range dependencies do not degrade. **3. Uniform, hardware-friendly compute.** A transformer is overwhelmingly large dense matrix multiplications, which run at near-peak efficiency on modern accelerators. **4. Predictable scaling laws.** Kaplan et al. (2020) found that loss follows a power law in parameters, data, and compute — smooth, extrapolable curves. That predictability is what justified spending ₹800 crore on a single training run: you could forecast the result before starting. **The cost:** attention is O(n²) in sequence length. Doubling context quadruples compute and memory, which is why context windows were 512 tokens in 2018 and why extending them has required serious engineering — FlashAttention for memory-efficient exact attention, sliding-window and sparse patterns for approximations, and grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache. | | RNN | Transformer | |---|---|---| | Training parallelism | None | Full | | Path between positions | O(n) | O(1) | | Compute per layer | O(n·d²) | O(n²·d + n·d²) | | Memory in inference | O(1) | O(n) KV cache | | Scales with compute | Poorly | Predictably | ##### Common mistakes - **Forgetting positional encoding**, leaving the model permutation-invariant. - **Post-norm in a deep model** without careful warm-up. - **Omitting residual connections**, reintroducing vanishing gradients. - **Applying the causal mask after softmax** instead of setting scores to `-inf` first. - **Using BatchNorm** instead of LayerNorm for sequences. - **Sequences longer than `block_size`**, indexing past the positional embedding table. - **Forgetting to shift targets by one** for next-token prediction — a bug that produces suspiciously low loss. - **`d_model` not divisible by `n_heads`.** - **No warm-up**, causing early-training divergence. - **Ignoring the O(n²) memory cost** and running out of GPU memory at long context. - **Believing the encoder-decoder diagram is what GPT looks like.** GPT is the decoder stack only, without cross-attention. ##### Hands-on: annotate, then build Your practical task is reading Jay Alammar's *The Illustrated Transformer* and annotating a diagram with each component's purpose. Do it as a real exercise rather than a skim: for each box, write one sentence saying what would break without it. "Remove positional encoding → the model cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'." "Remove residual connections → gradients vanish past about six layers." That annotated diagram is a reference you will return to for years. The mini project follows Karpathy's *Let's build GPT* lecture to build a character-level nanoGPT. This is the most valuable two hours in this entire course. Type the code rather than cloning it — the friction is the point. By the end you will have a working transformer under 300 lines, trained on Shakespeare, generating text that is recognisably Shakespeare-shaped. Then swap the corpus for something Indian: Tagore's translated poems, a collection of Bollywood song lyrics, or the Indian Constitution. Watching your own transformer learn the rhythms of a text you chose is what makes the architecture feel real. The assignment summarises *Attention Is All You Need* in your own words. Write it for someone who knows Days 18–21 but has not read the paper. Cover the motivation (RNN parallelism limits), the mechanism (self-attention, QKV, multi-head), the supporting pieces (positional encoding, FFN, residuals, LayerNorm), and the results. Then add a paragraph the paper could not have written: what happened next, and why the parallelism claim mattered more than the BLEU scores. ##### Key takeaways - **The transformer's real breakthrough was parallelism**, not accuracy — removing recurrence let training scale with hardware, which is what made large language models economically possible. - **Attention is permutation-invariant**, so positional information must be injected — via sinusoids, learned embeddings, or RoPE in modern models. - **Attention moves information between positions; the feedforward network processes it within a position** — and the FFN holds about two-thirds of the parameters. - **Residual connections plus pre-norm LayerNorm are what make deep stacks trainable**; without them 96-layer models would not converge. - **Encoder-only for understanding, decoder-only for generation, encoder-decoder for transformation** — and decoder-only won because good enough next-token prediction subsumes nearly everything.
